rationale: Choice C is the best answer because it most logically completes the text’s discussion of the evolution of mammalian brain-to-body size ratios. rationale: Choice D is the best answer because it most logically completes the text’s discussion of how The Adventures of Indiana Jones in Wenceslas Square in Prague on January 16, 1989 was originally distributed. The text goes on to contrast the game’s original distribution with its current broader availability. This context supports the idea that copies were originally distributed surreptitiously—that is, secretly, as would be necessary for an act of protest against an authoritarian regime. The text describes the game as an act of political protest, suggesting that its creation and distribution were motivated by strong feelings about the then Czechoslovakian regime. Moreover, the text establishes the contrast between secretive distribution and open availability, not between emotional and unemotional distribution. Choice C is incorrect because saying that copies of the game were originally distributed “disingenuously,” or in an insincere manner, wouldn’t make sense in this context. The text characterizes the game as a sincere act of political protest, and the contrast the text sets up concerns secrecy (“underground” and “anonymously”) versus openness (“readily available”).

question: Text 1 Hycean planets are a class of exoplanets (planets outside our solar system) with oceans of liquid water—critical to supporting life—and atmospheres rich in hydrogen. By observing that unlike the hycean candidate Madhusudhan et al. discovered, most other types of planets with hydrogen-rich atmospheres are likely located within the HZ

Based on this characterization of the HZ, Madhusudhan et al. identified K2-18 b as a hycean candidate whose location falls on the “inner edge” of the HZ—implying that its distance from its star is about 1 AU. rationale: Step 1: Find the structural cue. The sentence pivots on but . The axis is durability of memory — how securely each woman is held in historical memory. Kwolek's memory is secure and lasting. Pennington's, per the contrast, must be less secure. It makes Pennington's memory more secure than Kwolek's, which flatly contradicts but plus "will long be remembered." D. prominent — measures visibility or fame, not durability, and again points the wrong way: it would make Pennington the better-remembered of the two. B. tentative — means provisional, not firmly settled. It is on the durability axis and points in the direction but demands. Say the axis out loud ("how lastingly each is remembered") and the direction ("less secure than Kwolek") before looking at the options, then kill every choice on a different axis — warranted dies immediately under that test. Passage (no passage) Question The result of increasing the quantity \(x\) by \(400\%\) is \(60\). What is the value of \(x\)?
rationale: Step 1: Write the multiplier before doing anything else. Increasing a quantity by \(p\%\) multiplies it by \(\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\) — the original amount is still there, and the increase is added on top. For \(p = 400\): \(1 + \frac{400}{100} = 1 + 4 = 5\). So "increased by 400%" means ×5 , not ×4. Step 2: Solve. \(5x = 60 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 12\). Step 3: Check. \(12 \times 5 = 60\). Confirm it reads correctly as a percent increase: the increase itself is \(60 - 12 = 48\), and \(\frac{48}{12} = 4 = 400\%\). The increase is 400% of the original , exactly as stated. Why the distractors fail: B. 15 — the choice actually selected, and the whole point of the question. It comes from reading "400%" as the multiplier itself: \(4x = 60 \Rightarrow x = 15\). But ×4 is what "increased by 300 %" means, since \(1 + 3 = 4\). Checking would have caught it: \(15 \to 60\) is an increase of \(45\), and \(\frac{45}{15} = 3 = 300\%\). C. 20 — treating the phrase as "increased to 300%" or otherwise dividing by 3. Neither matches the wording. D. 240 — multiplying instead of dividing (\(60 \times 4\)), i.e. running the operation in the wrong direction. \(60\) is already the result , so \(x\) must be smaller than \(60\); any answer above \(60\) is eliminable on sight. Takeaway rule: never let a percent go straight into the equation. Write the multiplier on paper first — increase by \(p\%\) → \(\times\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\) , decrease by \(p\%\) → \(\times\left(1 - \frac{p}{100}\right)\) — then substitute. Percentages above 100 are where this leaks: +100% is ×2, +200% is ×3, +400% is ×5. Explanation written by Claude. Math · Hard · Problem Solving & Data Analysis · Percentages Trap you fell for: B. Read 400% as the multiplier (×4) instead of the increase (×5).

rationale: Step 1 — Translate the comparison. 'The length (x) is 7 more than the width (w).' Write it as an equation: x = w + 7. Solving for w: w = x − 7. Step 2 — Write the volume formula. Volume of a rectangular prism = length × width × height = x · (x − 7) · 9 = 9x(x − 7). So V(x) = 9x(x − 7). Step 3 — Why C fails. C uses x + 7, which would mean the width is x + 7. But 'x is 7 MORE THAN the width' means x is the larger quantity, so width = x − 7, not x + 7. Choosing + 7 reverses the comparison direction — the same direction-of-comparison flip logged in the PT6 variable-order loss. Step 4 — Confirm D. V(x) = 9x(x − 7): height 9, length x, width x − 7. Plug in a test: if x = 10, then width = 3. Volume = 9 · 10 · 3 = 270. Check: length (10) is 7 more than width (3) ✓. V(10) = 9·10·3 = 270 ✓. Rule: Always translate 'A is N more than B' as an equation (A = B + N → B = A − N) before substituting. Never read the comparison direction from the English directly into a formula without the intermediate step. Explanation written by Claude. Math · Hard · Advanced Math · Nonlinear functions

The right clause EXPLAINS 'indiscriminate' — 'notoriously indiscriminate: they will devour…' The right side defines/illustrates the adjective on the left. This is a classic colon use: left clause, colon, explanation/definition. Step 4 — Why B (the chosen wrong answer) fails. A comma between two independent clauses creates a comma splice. 'Goats are notoriously indiscriminate, they will devour…' — two full clauses, only a comma: that's a run-on. Eliminated. Step 5 — Why A fails. 'Indiscriminate and they will devour…' — 'and' joins clauses, but the result is clunky and doesn't convey the explanatory relationship. Step 6 — Why C fails. No punctuation between two independent clauses is a fused/run-on sentence. Step 7 — Why D is correct. Left side (independent clause) + colon + right side (explanation of 'indiscriminate'). The colon signals 'here is what I mean by that word.' ✓ Pattern note: When the right clause explains a specific word in the left clause, a colon is almost always correct. Passage While recent scholarship has undermined claims that the works of the twelfth-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd (Averroes) were ______ other Muslim philosophers of his time, it is indisputable that his geographic location meant his works were primarily available through Latin translations in Europe rather than in the Islamic world. Question Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
rationale: Step 1 — Parse the sentence structure. 'Scholarship has UNDERMINED CLAIMS THAT his works were [blank] other Muslim philosophers.' This is a double negative: scholarship undermines the claim. So the blank holds the OLD CLAIM, which is now being disproved. Step 2 — What does the rest of the sentence tell us? 'His works were primarily available through Latin translations in Europe rather than in the Islamic world.' This implies his works did not circulate widely among Muslim philosophers — his influence on that group was limited/minimal. Step 3 — What was the claim being undermined? The claim that his works were [blank] other Muslim philosophers. The second half tells us his works weren't available to them → so the OLD CLAIM must have been that he DID have some impact on them. But the double-negative says: scholarship now undermines the claim that he mattered to them. So the blank = 'consequential/influential' or at minimum NOT 'inconsequential.' Wait — actually, reversed: the claim being undermined is that he WAS inconsequential to them. Scholarship shows he actually WAS consequential. OR: scholarship undermines the claim that he WAS consequential. The second-half evidence (works only reached via Latin) supports 'inconsequential.' Re-read: scholarship undermines claims that his works were [blank] to/among other Muslim philosophers. If blank = 'inconsequential to,' then the claim being undermined is 'his works were inconsequential to Muslim philosophers.' Since scholarship undermines this claim, scholarship shows he WAS consequential. But the second half says his works circulated mainly in Europe — contradicting consequential impact in the Islamic world. The correct reading: scholarship undermines the claim he was inconsequential → he WAS impactful. But his works reached Europe, not the Islamic world. This is consistent: his European influence was great; the claim that he was inconsequential (to Muslim philosophy broadly) is what's being revised. Why C fails: 'imitated by' means Muslim philosophers copied his work. The sentence structure shows this claim is being undermined (shown false). But there's no logical reason the second clause (about Latin translations in Europe) specifically undermines 'imitated by.' D fits the logic better. Why D is correct: 'inconsequential to other Muslim philosophers' was the old claim (now undermined by scholarship showing he was actually consequential). His works reached them mainly via Europe, but scholars now recognize his influence on the broader tradition. D passes the logical-structure test. ✓ Key technique: bracket 'scholarship has undermined claims that' and focus on what the second clause implies about the blank. Then test each choice. Explanation written by Claude. Reading & Writing · Hard · Information and Ideas · Words in Context

rationale: Step 1 — Map each sentence to a structural role (the sentence-role technique). Sentence 1: '…though how deep these effects extend is unclear.' → GAP (knowledge gap / open question). Sentence 2: 'Hypothesizing that differences in land use lead to…' → HYPOTHESIS. Sentence 3: '…researchers collected soil samples…' → METHOD. Step 2 — Read the labels back: gap → hypothesis → method → finding(confirm). Match to choices. Why A fails: A says 'conflicting conclusions drawn by different scientists.' The text never mentions different scientists or conflicting conclusions — only one research group, and their result confirmed (not disputed) the hypothesis. Why B is correct: gap + hypothesis + method + confirming finding = B's description exactly. ✓ Why C fails: The passage opens by noting the question is unclear ('though how deep…is unclear'), the opposite of an established consensus. question: Passage While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes: Medieval images communicate the status of individual people and figures using nuances of gaze and positioning. Less powerful figures such as saints and heroes gaze directly at a viewer and occupy side positions in an image. In a circa 550 CE icon from the Mount Sinai Monastery in Egypt, Saint Theodore and Saint George are depicted in this manner. More powerful figures such as angels gaze away from the viewer and are positioned towards the center of an image. In the Mount Sinai icon, two angels are depicted in this manner. Question The student wants to describe a contrast present in the Mount Sinai icon. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Traceable to the Mount Sinai Monastery, one circa 550 CE icon features Saint Theodore, Saint George, and two angels among the individuals that it depicts.
The two angels positioned at the center of the Mount Sinai icon look away from the viewer, while the saints towards the sides of the icon look directly at the viewer.
Gaze and positioning are central to images such as the Mount Sinai icon, which depicts two angels that look away from the viewer.
In the Mount Sinai icon, two saints look outward at the viewer, and two angels are situated towards the center of the icon itself.
answer: ["B \u2014 The two angels positioned at the center of the Mount Sinai icon look away from the viewer, while the saints towards the sides of the icon look directly at the viewer."]
rationale: Step 1 — Identify the goal: The student wants to describe a contrast within the Mount Sinai icon — how different figures are depicted based on their status. The correct choice must set the angels against the saints on both dimensions the notes track: gaze (toward vs. away) and position (center vs. side). Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Eliminate A: It merely lists who the icon depicts (Theodore, George, two angels). No contrast — no comparison of gaze or position. Off goal. Eliminate C: It states a general principle plus one fact (angels look away). It describes only the angels, not the saints, so there is no contrast. Half the comparison is missing. Eliminate D: It gets the details backwards/incomplete — it says the saints look outward (true) and the angels are toward the center (true) but omits the angels' gaze away , and more importantly it doesn't frame the two facts as opposed. It reads as a list, not a contrast, and drops the angels' averted gaze that is the sharpest point of difference. Confirm B: It explicitly pits the two groups against each other — angels at the center look away , saints at the sides look directly at the viewer. Both the gaze axis and the position axis are contrasted in one sentence, exactly matching the notes. Only B delivers the contrast. Passage Octopuses can navigate mazes, open sealed jars, and recall which handlers have treated them badly, feats that imply considerable intelligence. Their neural architecture, ___, looks nothing like a vertebrate's: roughly two-thirds of their neurons sit in their arms rather than in a central brain. Question Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rationale: Run the direction test first. Sentence 1 says octopuses act intelligent, which sets up the expectation that they are built like other intelligent animals. Sentence 2 says their nervous system looks nothing like a vertebrate's. Expectation defeated equals CONTRAST. Choice A asserts the odd architecture follows from the intelligence — it does not. Choice C offers the arm-neuron fact as an example of intelligence, but it is an example of different wiring , not of clever behaviour. Choice D stacks the two sentences as agreeing points, ignoring "nothing like." Rule: predict sentence 2 from sentence 1 before you look at the choices. If reality contradicts the prediction, take the contrast word — this is the exact flip that cost you two questions on PT5.

question: Passage While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes: Located approximately 1,300 light-years from Earth, the GW Orionis star system consists of three stars. At the center of the system, two stars orbit one another. A more distant third star orbits these two central stars. This unusual arrangement impacted the alignment of the vast ring of material (known as a "protoplanetary disk") surrounding each of the stars. A ring of this sort normally surrounds a relatively young star and contains dust and gas that will eventually form into planets. Question The student wants to describe the arrangement of the stars in the GW Orionis system. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A protoplanetary disk surrounds each star in the GW Orionis system, and the presence of such a disk indicates that each one of the stars is relatively young.
Three stars, two of which orbit each other in a central pair and the third of which orbits the central two, form the GW Orionis system.
Unusual in the configuration of its stars, the GW Orionis star system is located roughly 1,300 light-years from Earth.
Taking the form of a vast ring of material, the protoplanetary disk of each star in the GW Orionis system consists of gas and dust.
answer: ["B \u2014 Three stars, two of which orbit each other in a central pair and the third of which orbits the central two, form the GW Orionis system."]
rationale: Step 1 — Identify the goal: The student wants to describe the arrangement of the stars — how the three stars are positioned relative to one another. The correct choice must convey the central pair plus the more distant third star. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Eliminate A: It's about the protoplanetary disk and the stars' youth, not how the stars are arranged. Off goal. Eliminate C: It gives the system's distance from Earth (1,300 light-years) and asserts the configuration is unusual without saying what the arrangement is. Distance ≠ arrangement. Off goal. Eliminate D: It describes the composition of the disk (gas and dust). Nothing about star positions. Off goal. Confirm B: It states exactly the arrangement — two stars orbiting each other as a central pair and a third orbiting that pair. This synthesizes the "two stars orbit one another" and "a more distant third star orbits these two" notes. Only B describes the stellar arrangement. question: Passage During the Meiji Restoration—a period of both return to tradition and rapid societal change—Japanese painter Uemura Shōen composed scenes that accord a new prominence to realistic female figures while revisiting time-honored techniques in sourcing paints and pigments. _ her works embody contrasts evident within the Restoration generally. Question Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rationale: Step 1: Analyze the first sentence. The first sentence describes how Uemura Shōen's work combines two opposing elements: a return to tradition and rapid societal change. It specifies that she uses realistic female figures (a new approach) alongside time-honored techniques (a traditional approach). Step 2: Analyze the second sentence. The second sentence observes that Shōen's works embody contrasts that were present throughout the Meiji Restoration in general. This statement serves to emphasize or confirm the observation made in the first sentence by connecting her specific artistic choices to a broader historical context. Step 3: Eliminate option A. That being said is used to introduce a contrasting or qualifying point. However, the second sentence supports and reinforces the first rather than contradicting it. Step 4: Eliminate option B. Even more importantly suggests a hierarchy of importance between two different points. The second sentence is a summary or conclusion of the first, not necessarily a more important piece of information. Step 5: Eliminate option C. In addition is used to introduce a completely new, separate fact. The second sentence explains the significance of the facts already provided in the first sentence. Step 6: Confirm the correct answer. The transition Indeed is used to emphasize or provide further evidence for a point just made. Since the second sentence summarizes how Shōen's work reflects the broader spirit of the Meiji Restoration described in the first sentence, Indeed provides the most logical connection. Therefore, the answer is D. Source: OnePrep explanation. Reading & Writing · Medium · Expression of Ideas · Transitions

question: Passage While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes: A pottery wheel enables artisans and craft makers to create symmetrical shapes. Step 1: A potter will secure or "throw" a piece of wet clay into the middle of a potter wheel. Step 2: The potter will spin the pottery wheel either manually (using a foot pedal) or automatically (if the pottery wheel is attached to an electric motor that enables rotation). Step 3: As the wheel is spinning, the potter will shape the clay by hand (making sure to keep the clay moist as it turns) or using implements known as rib tools. Step 4: The clay will be cut from the wheel using a thin metal wire in preparation for baking (which will harden the clay) and further decoration. Question The student wants to summarize how a pottery wheel operates. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: After "throwing" a piece of clay to secure it to the wheel, a potter will spin a pottery wheel while shaping the clay by hand or by using rib tools.
Pottery clay can be attached to a pottery wheel through "throwing" and removed through cutting with a thin metal wire.
A pottery wheel will spin in one of two manners: a potter can use a foot pedal, or an electric motor can cause the wheel to rotate automatically.
Once a piece of clay pottery has been removed from a pottery wheel, a potter can bake the pottery to ensure that the clay will harden.
answer: ["A \u2014 After \"throwing\" a piece of clay to secure it to the wheel, a potter will spin a pottery wheel while shaping the clay by hand or by using rib tools."]
rationale: Step 1: Identify the student's goal. The student wants to summarize how a pottery wheel operates . To do this effectively, the chosen answer must capture the essential sequence of the operation: securing the clay, spinning the wheel, and shaping the object. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Define the test. On a Rhetorical Synthesis question the goal sentence is the whole test. "Summarize how it operates" demands breadth — the answer must span the process, not report one isolated stage. Any choice that is factually accurate but covers only a single step fails the goal even though it fails no fact-check. Step 3: Eliminate B. True but incomplete. B mentions attaching the clay (Step 1) and cutting it off (Step 4) but skips the spinning and shaping that are the actual operation of the wheel. It describes how clay gets on and off the wheel, not how the wheel works. Step 4: Eliminate C. True but too narrow. C covers only Step 2, the two ways the wheel can be made to spin. It's a detail about the wheel's power source, not a summary of the process. Step 5: Eliminate D. True but out of scope. D describes what happens after the clay leaves the wheel — baking and hardening. That is post-wheel finishing, so it cannot summarize how the wheel operates. Step 6: Confirm A. A chains Steps 1 → 2 → 3 in order: throw the clay to secure it, spin the wheel, shape the clay by hand or with rib tools. It is the only choice that traces the operation across multiple stages, so it is the only one that meets the stated goal. Reading & Writing · Hard · Expression of Ideas · Rhetorical Synthesis

question: Passage (no passage) Question Circle A in the xy-plane has the equation (x − 8)² + (y + 12)² = 9. Circle B has the same center as circle A. The radius of circle B is four times the radius of circle A. The equation defining circle B in the xy-plane is (x − 8)² + (y + 12)² = k, where k is a constant. What is the value of k? Student-produced response (no multiple-choice options). Correct answer: 144
rationale: Circle A is written in standard form (x − h)² + (y − j)² = r², so its radius satisfies r_A² = 9, giving r_A = 3. Circle B has radius four times that of circle A: r_B = 4 · 3 = 12. Circle B's equation has the same center, so k plays the role of r_B². Therefore k = r_B² = 12² = 144 . Watch the trap: k is not 4 × 9 = 36. Scaling the radius by 4 scales r² by 4² = 16, so k = 9 · 16 = 144. Explanation written by Claude. Math · Hard · Geometry and Trigonometry · Circles

question: Passage (no passage) Question A cube has a volume of 1,124,864 cubic units. What is the surface area, in square units, of the cube? Student-produced response (no multiple-choice options). Correct answer: 64,896
rationale: For a cube with edge length s: volume = s³ and surface area = 6s². Find the edge from the volume: s = ∛1,124,864 = 104 (since 104³ = 104 · 104 · 104 = 1,124,864). Then surface area = 6s² = 6 · 104² = 6 · 10,816 = 64,896 square units. Common error: stopping at s² = 10,816 (one face) or forgetting the factor of 6. Six faces, so multiply by 6. Explanation written by Claude. Math · Hard · Geometry and Trigonometry · Area and volume

passage: Passage True to its name, National Buy Nothing Day encourages consumers to refrain from new purchases for 24 _ the efficacy of such restraint—particularly over the long term—is open to dispute. Buy Nothing Day is arguably too fleeting to change ingrained spending habits and may, by briefly stifling purchases, inadvertently prompt consumers to make catch-up purchases after the 24 hours conclude. Question Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question: Passage True to its name, National Buy Nothing Day encourages consumers to refrain from new purchases for 24 _ the efficacy of such restraint—particularly over the long term—is open to dispute. Buy Nothing Day is arguably too fleeting to change ingrained spending habits and may, by briefly stifling purchases, inadvertently prompt consumers to make catch-up purchases after the 24 hours conclude. Question Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rationale: Step 1: Identify the two clauses. The sentence consists of two distinct ideas: the goal of National Buy Nothing Day and the debate regarding its actual effectiveness. These are two independent clauses that could stand as separate sentences. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Decide what job "though" is doing. "Though" can work two ways: as a subordinating conjunction ("though X is true, Y") or as a parenthetical adverb ("Y, though, is true"). Here it sits at the front of the second clause, so it must be read as a subordinating conjunction — it converts "the efficacy of such restraint... is open to dispute" into a dependent clause. A dependent clause can be joined to the preceding independent clause with a single comma. Correctly punctuated: "…refrain from new purchases for 24 hours, though the efficacy of such restraint—particularly over the long term—is open to dispute." Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. C. hours, — with "though" removed, you have two full independent clauses joined by only a comma. That is a comma splice. A. hours, though; — the semicolon must separate two independent clauses. Placing it after "though" strands "though" at the end of the first clause (where it reads as a trailing adverb) and then requires the second clause to stand alone, producing a garbled boundary. You cannot follow a subordinating conjunction with a semicolon. D. hours, though, — the pair of commas turns "though" into a parenthetical aside, which means it no longer subordinates the second clause. Strip the aside and you are back to two independent clauses joined by a comma — a comma splice again. B. hours, though — one comma, "though" attached to the clause it subordinates. Correct. Takeaway rule: for Boundaries items, first mark each side of the blank as independent (I) or dependent (D). I + I needs a period, semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS. I + D takes just a comma. Then check whether the connector word is inside the second clause (subordinator) or fenced off by commas (parenthetical) — that single distinction decides A/B/D here. question: Reconstructed question. The original source page was not stored. This is an authored reconstruction built from the logged setup, the correct answer, and the saved rule — not the original wording. The coach's original phrasing was defective; this version states the construction cleanly. Passage (no passage) Question In the figure, \(\overline{PT}\) is tangent to the circle at point \(T\). The radius of the circle is \(9\), and the distance from the center \(O\) to the external point \(P\) is \(15\). What is the length of \(\overline{PT}\)?
rationale: Step 1: Use the tangent–radius property. A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency. So angle \(OTP\) is a right angle, and triangle \(OTP\) is a right triangle with the right angle at \(T\) — not at \(O\) and not at \(P\). Step 2: Identify the hypotenuse correctly. The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle, so it is \(\overline{OP}\), the center-to-external-point distance of \(15\). The radius \(9\) and the tangent \(PT\) are the two legs. Step 3: Solve. \(PT = \sqrt{OP^2 - OT^2} = \sqrt{15^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{225 - 81} = \sqrt{144} = 12\). Why the distractors fail: C. \(\sqrt{306}\) — the single most common error: treating \(15\) as a leg and adding (\(\sqrt{15^2+9^2}\)). This happens when the right angle is placed at \(O\) instead of at \(T\). If \(15\) is the distance to the center , it must be the longest side. A. 6 — subtracting the lengths directly (\(15 - 9\)) instead of using the Pythagorean theorem. This is the distance from \(P\) to the near edge of the circle along line \(OP\), a different segment entirely. D. 24 — adding the lengths (\(15 + 9\)), the distance from \(P\) to the far edge of the circle along line \(OP\). Also not the tangent. Takeaway rule: on any circle-plus-external-point problem, draw the radius to the point of tangency first. That radius is perpendicular to the tangent, which fixes the hypotenuse as the center-to-point distance. Then \(\text{tangent} = \sqrt{d^2 - r^2}\). Explanation written by Claude. A circle with center \(O\) and radius \(9\). An external point \(P\) lies \(15\) units from \(O\). Segment \(PT\) is drawn from \(P\) so that it touches the circle at exactly one point, \(T\) (the point of tangency). Radius \(OT\) is drawn to that point, forming triangle \(OTP\) with \(OT = 9\) and \(OP = 15\). question: Passage During her early career as a field botanist, Dr. Lian Duarte focused primarily on documenting plant species in remote wetlands. After several seasons of survey work, she was invited to assist regional planners who hoped to stabilize riverbanks damaged by decades of erosion. Through this collaboration, Duarte eventually served as a senior advisor on the __ of riparian zones across multiple counties, helping officials restore ecological function while preserving native plant diversity. Question Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
rationale: Step 1: Analyze the context. The passage describes Dr. Duarte's work helping officials stabilize riverbanks damaged by decades of erosion and restore ecological function. We are looking for a word that describes the process of fixing or restoring an environment that has been damaged. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Nail the requirement from the surrounding phrases. Two phrases define the blank: "damaged by decades of erosion" (the problem) and "helping officials restore ecological function" (the goal). So the blank names the repair of environmental damage — and it must be a noun that takes "of riparian zones." Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. A. recalibration — means readjusting an instrument or a standard to a correct setting. It implies fine-tuning something that is merely off-target, not repairing something damaged . Also, you recalibrate a measurement or a policy, not a physical landscape. C. remuneration — means payment for work or services. A pure sound-alike trap: it shares the "rem-" opening with "remediation" but belongs to the domain of compensation, not restoration. Nothing in the passage concerns money. D. redirection — means changing the course or aim of something. You could redirect a river, but the passage is about restoring ecological function and preserving native plant diversity , not rerouting anything. Wrong action. B. remediation — the standard environmental term for correcting or reversing damage to a site. It matches "damaged by decades of erosion" + "restore ecological function" exactly, and "remediation of riparian zones" is idiomatic. Takeaway rule: on hard Words-in-Context items the distractors are often near-homophones of the answer ("remuneration" vs "remediation"). Before choosing, state the required meaning in plain English in your own words first ("fixing damaged land"), then check each option against that phrase — never against how the word sounds. question: Passage Materials that are themselves organic _ in next-generation solar panels to facilitate both plant growth and efficient energy production, as scientists at the University of California, Los Angeles have discovered. Researchers have constructed a greenhouse with a roof formed partially of transparent organic solar cells that convert some sunlight to solar energy while allowing a portion of the sun's rays to pass through and nurture the plants below. Question Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rationale: Step 1: Identify the main subject. The phrase Materials that are themselves organic serves as the subject. For the sentence to be complete, we need a main (finite) verb to follow this subject. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: See why the sentence currently has no verb. Strip the relative clause "that are themselves organic" (its verb are belongs to that , not to Materials ). What remains is "Materials _ in next-generation solar panels…" — the blank is the only slot left for the sentence's main verb. So the answer must be a finite verb phrase , not an infinitive or a bare participle. Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. A. to be incorporated — an infinitive. Infinitives are non-finite and cannot serve as a main verb, leaving the sentence a fragment: "Materials… to be incorporated in solar panels." C. to incorporate — also an infinitive, and additionally wrong in voice: the materials are the things being incorporated, not the agent doing the incorporating. B. incorporated — the strongest trap. Standing alone after the subject it can be read as a past participle continuing the modifier chain ("Materials that are themselves organic, incorporated in…"), which again yields a fragment. Even read as a simple past tense, it wrongly asserts that this has already been done, whereas the passage frames it as a discovered possibility demonstrated by a prototype greenhouse. D. could be incorporated — a finite modal verb phrase in the passive voice. It gives the subject a real main verb and matches the passage's meaning: scientists discovered that this is possible. Takeaway rule: when the blank is the sentence's only candidate for a main verb, cross out every relative clause and modifier first, then ask "does what's left have a subject and a conjugated verb?" Infinitives (to + verb) and bare participles can never fill that slot. Reading & Writing · Hard · Standard English Conventions · Form, Structure, and Sense

question: Passage While searching for the elusive long-beaked echidna—one of half a dozen living mammals known _ eggs—a team of researchers from Oxford University and several universities in Indonesia performed an intensive review of the ecology of Indonesia's Cyclops Mountains, the home habitat of this critically-endangered small mammal. Question Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rationale: Step 1: Analyze the sentence structure. The sentence uses a descriptive phrase starting with the word known to explain a key characteristic of the living mammals. In Standard English, we need a specific verb form to follow this participle to complete the modifier correctly. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Recognize the fixed construction. The phrase between the dashes — "one of half a dozen living mammals known _ eggs" — is an appositive modifying echidna . Inside it, "known" is a past participle, and the idiom in Standard English is known to + base verb ("known to lay," "known to migrate," "known to exist"). The appositive has no subject of its own, so it cannot host a conjugated verb. Step 3: Rule out each wrong choice. D. lays — a finite present-tense verb. It would need a subject, but the appositive already ends at "mammals"; inserting a conjugated verb creates "mammals known lays eggs," which is ungrammatical. (Also singular lays against plural mammals .) C. is laying — likewise finite, and the progressive wrongly suggests the action is happening right now rather than being a general species trait. A. laying — the tempting one, since "known" is often followed by a gerund elsewhere. But "known laying eggs" is not idiomatic; "known for laying eggs" would need the preposition for , which is not offered. Without for , the participle cannot attach. B. to lay — completes the standard "known to [verb]" idiom and correctly expresses a general characteristic of the species. Takeaway rule: when a blank follows a participle like known , said , thought , believed , or reported , the SAT is almost always testing the "known/said/thought to + base verb" idiom. Check whether the clause has a subject available; if it doesn't, any conjugated verb form is automatically out. Reading & Writing · Hard · Standard English Conventions · Form, Structure, and Sense

The narrator, a reclusive poet in his late thirties, reflects on a habit he developed during long periods of solitude. I often spent entire weeks tucked away in my rented attic room, writing until the daylight thinned and the streetlamps glowed through the frost. Yet, without fail, some inner pull would send me downstairs to the bakery on the corner, where I would trade a few polite words with the owner. The moment I stepped inside, however, a strange stillness overtook me; I felt both rooted to the threshold and quietly relieved, as though the world's noise had dimmed just enough to let me breathe. options: To illustrate how the narrator's brief excursions into public spaces create a paradoxical blend of tension and solace
To reveal the narrator's frustration with the monotony of his writing routine and his longing for constant social attention
To suggest that the narrator's encounters at the bakery sparked a dramatic shift in his creative ambitions
To emphasize the narrator's dependence on the bakery owner for emotional guidance and personal affirmation
answer: ["A \u2014 To illustrate how the narrator's brief excursions into public spaces create a paradoxical blend of tension and solace"]
rationale: Step 1: Identify the narrator's routine. The text begins by establishing the narrator's lifestyle: a reclusive poet spending weeks in an attic room, suggesting a high degree of solitude. However, he describes an inner pull that leads him to a brief, regular interaction at a local bakery. Step 2: Analyze the bakery experience. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). The structural cue is the paired, contradictory language in the third sentence: "I felt both rooted to the threshold and quietly relieved." Being rooted (frozen, unable to move further in) is tension; relief and the world's noise dimming is solace. The final sentence adds that the interruption "soften[ed] the edges of my isolation" — a mild, ongoing effect, not a transformation. A main-purpose answer must capture that mixed, small-scale effect. B. gets the polarity wrong twice: the narrator expresses no frustration with his writing, and "longing for constant social attention" overshoots — he trades only "a few polite words." C. overstates the outcome. Nothing in the text mentions his creative ambitions changing, let alone dramatically; the effect described is emotional and modest. D. misplaces the focus. The owner is barely present, and the narrator seeks no guidance or affirmation from him; what matters is the experience of stepping into a public space. A. names both halves of the described feeling — tension ("rooted to the threshold") and solace ("quietly relieved," isolation softened) — and correctly calls the excursions brief, matching the scale of the text. options: Both Benton and Velasquez reimagine the historical tower as a site of mystery and concealment, though Benton focuses on government secrecy while Velasquez explores supernatural elements.

rationale: Step 1: Analyze the fictional uses. Benton changes the tower into a secret government listening post; Velasquez makes it a haunted broadcast site. Both represent a significant departure from its real-world history as a navigation tool. Step 2: Rule out historical roles. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). The goal has two requirements: (1) a conclusion covering both authors, and (2) support drawn only from the notes. C. contradicts the notes outright — neither novel keeps the tower as a working navigation facility, and neither is set during its operational era. B. accurately reports each author separately but never draws a shared conclusion; it is a side-by-side summary, not a claim about how both reinterpret the tower. It also adds "folklore about abandoned coastal structures," which the notes never mention. D. goes beyond the notes twice: nothing supports the claim that the authors comment on "changing attitudes toward technology," and calling Benton's spy premise "realistic" versus Velasquez's "fantastical" imposes a contrast the notes don't draw. passage: Passage At a movie theater, customers could buy tickets either at a self-service kiosk or at the ticket counter. On a certain evening, 25% of all customers used the kiosk, and the rest used the counter. Among the customers using the kiosk, 60% bought popcorn. Among the customers using the counter, 35% bought popcorn. Question Based on this information, which of the following is an accurate conclusion?
question: Passage At a movie theater, customers could buy tickets either at a self-service kiosk or at the ticket counter. On a certain evening, 25% of all customers used the kiosk, and the rest used the counter. Among the customers using the kiosk, 60% bought popcorn. Among the customers using the counter, 35% bought popcorn. Question Based on this information, which of the following is an accurate conclusion?
options: If all customers had used the kiosk, more customers would have bought popcorn.
Customers using the kiosk were more likely to be teenagers than customers using the counter.
If all customers who used the counter had instead used the kiosk, the same number of popcorn orders would have been sold.
Customers using the kiosk were more likely to buy popcorn than customers using the counter.
answer: ["D \u2014 Customers using the kiosk were more likely to buy popcorn than customers using the counter."]
rationale: Explanation written by Claude. Set up the numbers. Let the total number of customers be 100 for convenience. Kiosk: 25% of 100 = 25 customers. Of those, 60% bought popcorn → 0.60 × 25 = 15 popcorn buyers . Counter: the rest = 75 customers. Of those, 35% bought popcorn → 0.35 × 75 = 26.25 popcorn buyers . Note the trap: the counter group produced more popcorn sales in absolute terms (26.25 > 15), even though its rate is lower. What the data actually supports. The two percentages, 60% and 35%, are conditional rates — the probability of buying popcorn given which line you used. 60% > 35%, so a kiosk customer was more likely to buy popcorn than a counter customer. That is a comparison of rates, and it is exactly what the given information establishes. Rule out each wrong choice. A. This is a causal counterfactual. Moving everyone to the kiosk assumes the 60% rate would still hold for people who chose the counter — an unwarranted assumption. Association is not causation; the kiosk group may simply be the type of customer who buys popcorn. Out of scope. B. Age is never mentioned anywhere in the passage. No data on teenagers exists. Out of scope entirely. C. Testable and false. If all 100 customers used the kiosk at a 60% rate, popcorn orders would be 60 rather than the actual 15 + 26.25 = 41.25. "The same number" is contradicted by the arithmetic (and it also carries A's flawed causal assumption). D. A pure rate comparison, directly supported: 60% > 35%. It claims nothing about totals or causes. Answer: D. Math · Medium · Problem-Solving and Data Analysis · Percentages

question: Passage Over the past decade, cognitive load theory, once confined to controlled studies of classroom instruction, has evolved into a broader framework for analyzing how people process complex information under varying environmental pressures. Researchers in human–computer interaction now employ it to assess user interfaces that demand rapid attention shifts or simultaneous decision-making. Similar adaptations are emerging in museum design and public-policy communication, where designers aim to manage how audiences absorb dense visual and textual data. _, the theory is being reinterpreted less as a prescriptive model for teachers and more as a general science of cognitive economy across contexts. Question Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rationale: Step 1: Find the structural cue. The three sentences before the blank are a chain of expanding applications : cognitive load theory started "confined to controlled studies of classroom instruction," then moved to human–computer interaction, then to museum design and public-policy communication. The final sentence reports the consequence — the theory is now read as a general science rather than a teaching model. So the blank needs a transition meaning more and more over time , matching "Over the past decade," "now employ," and "are emerging." Step 2: Rule out each wrong choice. B. Collectively — signals that separate items are being summed into a single group ("Collectively, the three studies show…"). The last sentence is not adding up the three fields into one total; it is reporting a trend that keeps growing. Wrong logical operation, and it is the choice that reads plausibly only because three fields were just listed. D. Correspondingly — signals a matching or parallel change caused by something just stated ("Prices rose; correspondingly, demand fell"). The preceding sentence gives one more example of spread, not a cause that requires a paired effect elsewhere. A. Progressively — the closest trap. It means in stages, advancing step by step toward an endpoint , and it normally modifies degree within one process ("progressively harder," "progressively weaker"). The passage is not describing staged advancement along a single path; it is describing a rising number of separate domains adopting the theory. C. Increasingly — means to a greater and greater extent , which is exactly the growth-in-prevalence relationship the paragraph builds. Takeaway rule: for Transitions, name the relationship in plain English before looking at the options ("more and more fields keep doing this"), then test each word against that sentence. Near-synonyms such as progressively and increasingly differ in what they scale — stages of one process versus breadth of adoption. Explanation written by Claude. question: Passage The following text is adapted from Frances Hodgson Burnett's 1911 novel The Secret Garden. Mary Lennox is visiting her cousin Colin for the first time. Curious about life outdoors, Colin asks Mary what early mornings in the garden feel like. She begins describing the pale light and the stillness before the birds stir, then notices Colin's expression tighten as he listens. Although he urges her to continue, his voice grows strained, and Mary abruptly stops, uncertain whether she has offered comfort or touched a hidden vulnerability. Question Based on the passage, how does Mary relate to Colin during this exchange?
options: She tries to answer honestly but becomes unsure whether her description has unintentionally exposed something he had hoped to keep concealed.
She attempts to reassure him by downplaying the appeal of the outdoors, though she senses her efforts are not convincing him.
She grows frustrated that he refuses to accept her experience as genuine, leading her to cut the description short.
She deliberately withholds details about the garden because she anticipates that hearing too much would distress him.
answer: ["A \u2014 She tries to answer honestly but becomes unsure whether her description has unintentionally exposed something he had hoped to keep concealed."]
rationale: Step 1: Track the sequence of events. Colin asks; Mary begins describing the pale light and the stillness; she then notices his expression tighten; he urges her on but his voice is strained; she abruptly stops , "uncertain whether she has offered comfort or touched a hidden vulnerability." Two facts control the answer: she answers sincerely, and her stopping is caused by uncertainty about the effect of what she has already said. Step 2: Rule out each wrong choice. D. She deliberately withholds details… because she anticipates that hearing too much would distress him. — this is the trap, because it lands on the same emotion (his distress) but reverses the order and the intent. Mary does not anticipate anything; she reacts after noticing his face tighten, and the text says she is uncertain , not that she has judged the situation and chosen to hold back. "Deliberately" also contradicts "abruptly." B. She attempts to reassure him by downplaying the appeal of the outdoors. — she does the opposite: she describes the garden's light and stillness appealingly. Nothing in the text has her minimizing anything, and no reassurance is attempted. C. She grows frustrated that he refuses to accept her experience as genuine. — wrong emotion and wrong cause. Colin never disputes her account; he urges her to continue . Frustration appears nowhere; the stated feeling is uncertainty. A. She tries to answer honestly but becomes unsure whether her description has unintentionally exposed something he had hoped to keep concealed. — matches both halves: she answers sincerely, and "touched a hidden vulnerability" is precisely "exposed something he had hoped to keep concealed," with "uncertain" carried over as "becomes unsure." Takeaway rule: for Central Ideas & Details on a narrative, convert the final clause of the passage into your own words before reading the options — here, "she doesn't know if she helped or hurt him." Then reject any option that upgrades uncertainty into a decision (D) or swaps in an emotion the text never names (C). Explanation written by Claude. question: Passage The poet Tracy K. Smith works across multiple genres, composing poetry, memoir, essays, and the recurring themes of science, history, and American identity that appear throughout her writing. Smith has noted that her cross-genre approach allows her to examine these subjects from different formal perspectives. Question Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rationale: Step 1: Close the list, then look at what follows. The sentence is "Smith works across multiple genres, composing poetry, memoir, essays, and the recurring themes of science, history, and American identity that appear throughout her writing." Poetry, memoir, essays, and fiction is a four-item list serving as the object of composing . Everything after that list — "exploring the recurring themes…" — is a participial phrase describing what the composing does. The question is how to punctuate the seam between the list and that phrase. Step 2: Rule out each wrong choice. B. fiction exploring — with no comma, exploring the recurring themes becomes a restrictive modifier of fiction alone, so the sentence claims only her fiction explores those themes. That contradicts "themes… that appear throughout her writing " and quietly changes the meaning rather than breaking a rule, which is why it is the most attractive wrong answer. A. fiction. Exploring — ending the sentence at fiction leaves "Exploring the recurring themes… that appear throughout her writing." as a fragment: a participial phrase with no subject and no main verb. C. fiction and exploring — the list is already closed by and before fiction ; adding a second and forces exploring to be read as a fifth list item joined to four nouns. A gerund cannot be parallel to poetry, memoir, essays, fiction , so this is faulty parallelism. D. fiction, exploring — one comma ends the list and marks the participial phrase as nonrestrictive, so it modifies the whole act of composing across all four genres. That is the reading the rest of the sentence demands. Takeaway rule: when a blank sits between the last item of a list and an -ing phrase, ask what the -ing phrase is supposed to modify. Modifies just the last item → no comma. Modifies the whole clause → comma. Then check the surrounding sentence for a phrase like "throughout her writing" that settles which reading is intended. question: Passage In 2007, cognitive psychologist Dr. Helen Sato began tracking how early-childhood play environments influence spatial reasoning over time. The study's initial phase uncovered several developmental trends and had _ expanded when Sato introduced an additional line of research examining play-based approaches to mathematical problem-solving. Question Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
rationale: Step 1: Read what the "when" clause is doing. The sentence is "The study's initial phase uncovered several developmental trends and had expanded when Sato introduced an additional line of research." The when clause names the moment the expansion happened — the point at which the new research line was added. So the adverb in the blank has to place the expansion after the initial phase and at that moment , not before it and not spread across it. Step 2: Rule out each wrong choice. B. already — "had already expanded when X" means the expansion was finished before X occurred. That reverses the causal order the sentence sets up: the study expands because Sato adds the new line, so the expansion cannot precede it. This is the trap answer, because "had already" is such a common past-perfect pairing that it sounds right by reflex. C. gradually — right idea (growth over time), wrong shape. "Gradually" describes change spread continuously over a stretch, but when Sato introduced pins the expansion to a single event. A gradual process and a one-moment trigger conflict. D. briefly — wrong meaning altogether. It says the expansion lasted only a short time, which the passage never suggests; adding a new line of research is presented as a lasting broadening of scope. A. later — places the expansion after the initial phase and lets the when clause identify exactly when "later" was. Sequence and cause both line up. Takeaway rule: when a blank sits inside a past-perfect verb ( had verb-ed ) next to a when / after / by the time clause, the question is almost always about order of events . Draw the two events on a timeline first: does the blank push the action before the other event ( already ), after it ( later ), or across it ( gradually )? Then pick the one that matches the causal story. Explanation written by Claude. Reading & Writing · Hard · (domain not listed) · Boundaries

question: Passage Samuel Taylor Coleridge's 1797 poem "This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison" revolves around a narrator who has been separated from a group of friends. options: "I have lost / Beauties and feelings, such as would have been / Most sweet to my remembrance"
"They, meanwhile, / Friends, whom I never more may meet again, / On springy heath, along the hill-top edge, / Wander in gladness"
"A delight / Comes sudden on my heart, and I am glad / As I myself were there!"
"Henceforth I shall know / That Nature ne'er deserts the wise and pure"
answer: ["C \u2014 \u201cA delight / Comes sudden on my heart, and I am glad / As I myself were there!\u201d"]
rationale: Choice C is the best answer because this choice properly calls attention to all of the content designated in the prompt. The word "glad" indicates "fulfilling" emotions, while the expression "As I myself were there" directly indicates a "bond" with companions who are otherwise distant. Choice A is incorrect because evoking what the narrator has "lost" introduces a negative tone, not a positive tone of fulfillment. Choice B is incorrect because the narrator here acknowledges that the friends experience positive emotions but indicates that the friends are distant and may never be met "again," thus contradicting the idea of a bond across a distance. Choice D is incorrect because it introduces a general statement or lesson concerning nature while avoiding the topic of the "companions" entirely.

question: Passage "My Heart and I" by Elizabeth Barrett Browning was composed and published in the late 1800s. In this poem, the narrator traces profound feelings of isolation back to specific causes: Question Which quotation from "My Heart and I" most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: "We walked too straight for fortune's end, / We loved too true to keep a friend; / At last we're tired, my heart and I."
"So tired, so tired, my heart and I! / It was not thus in that old time / When Ralph sat with me 'neath the lime / To watch the sunset from the sky."
"Tired out we are, my heart and I. / Suppose the world brought diadems / To tempt us, crusted with loose gems / Of powers and pleasures?"

answer: ["A \u2014 \u201cWe walked too straight for fortune's end, / We loved too true to keep a friend; / At last we're tired, my heart and I.\u201d"]
rationale: Choice A is the best answer because it looks to the past, explaining how the narrator and her heart have experienced disappointment as a result of trying to act with integrity ("we loved too true to keep a friend"). This perspective on previous disappointments explains why the narrator now feels isolated ("At last, we're tired"). Choice B is incorrect because it contrasts the narrator's current state of isolation ("so tired, so tired") with an earlier time when she was much more positive and open ("it was not thus in old times"). Choice C is incorrect because it shows the narrator musing on a hypothetical situation ("suppose the world brought diadems") but does not address the cause of her current isolation. Choice D is incorrect because it represents a change of perspective in which the speaker chastises herself for lamenting her unhappiness and isolation.

question: Passage \(4x^2 - 32x + 4y^2 + 24y - 80 = 0\) Question The equation above gives the graph of a circle in the \(xy\)-plane. If the circle is inscribed in a square, what is the area of the square? Student-produced response (grid-in). Correct answer: 180 — CORRECT Your answer: 20 ← your answer
rationale: The answer is 180. \(4x^2 - 32x + 4y^2 + 24y - 80 = 0\) \(x^2 - 8x + y^2 + 6y - 20 = 0\) \((x^2 - 8x + 16) + (y^2 + 6y + 9) = 20 + 16 + 9\) \((x - 4)^2 + (y + 3)^2 = 45\) \(r = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\) For a circle inscribed in a square, the side length of the square is the diameter. \(s = 2r = 6\sqrt{5}\) \(\text{Area of square} = s^2 = (6\sqrt{5})^2 = 180\)

question: Passage (no passage) Question The function g is defined by g(x) = 5x + c(x + 4), where c is a constant, and g(2) = 46. What is the value of g(5)? Student-produced response (no answer choices). Correct value: 79
rationale: Explanation written by Claude. Method 1 — solve for c, then evaluate. Substitute x = 2 into the definition: g(2) = 5(2) + c(2 + 4) = 10 + 6c Set that equal to the given value: 10 + 6c = 46 → 6c = 36 → c = 6 Now evaluate at x = 5: g(5) = 5(5) + 6(5 + 4) = 25 + 6(9) = 25 + 54 = 79 Method 2 — direct difference (faster, no need to isolate c). Expand once: g(x) = 5x + cx + 4c = (5 + c)x + 4c. This is linear in x with slope (5 + c), so g(5) − g(2) = (5 + c)(5 − 2) = 3(5 + c) You still need c, but note the slope shortcut is only a win once c is known — from 10 + 6c = 46, c = 6, so slope = 11 and g(5) = 46 + 3(11) = 46 + 33 = 79 . Where this goes wrong on test day. The two common errors are (1) distributing c only onto x and forgetting the +4c term, and (2) solving for c correctly but then plugging x = 5 back into the original g(2) equation instead of re-evaluating. Always rewrite the function in a clean form before substituting the second value. Math · Medium · Algebra · Linear functions

options: To describe the actions resulting from Marcel's high regard for "Passage of the Red Sea"
To call attention to some of the unusual features of Marcel's best-known picture
To explain why the salon judges reject "Passage of the Red Sea" despite Marcel's efforts
To illustrate how Marcel and the salon judges have attempted to arrive at a compromise
answer: ["A \u2014 To describe the actions resulting from Marcel's high regard for \"Passage of the Red Sea\""]
rationale: Step 1: Analyze Marcel's perspective. The passage begins by establishing Marcel's extremely high opinion of his own work, "The Passage of the Red Sea." He views it as a worthy companion to the famous masterpiece "Wedding of Cana." Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Connect opinion to actions. The structural hinge is "Accordingly" — because Marcel rates the picture so highly, he keeps resubmitting it each year, and then disguises it (modifying details, changing the title) to slip past the jury. Opinion → consequent behavior is the shape of the whole passage. Step 3: Eliminate B. The text never describes the picture's features — we learn nothing about its composition or subject beyond the title. It also never says this is his "best-known" picture. Step 4: Eliminate C. The passage says the jury seems to have "adopted a policy of exclusion" toward the painting, but it never explains why they reject it. Marcel is deceiving the examiners ("throw the examiners off the track"), and the judges are not portrayed as negotiating at all — the relationship is adversarial and one-sided. Step 6: Confirm A. A captures both halves: Marcel's high regard (his settled opinion that it rivals the "Wedding of Cana") and the resulting actions (annual resubmission plus cosmetic disguise). passage: Passage (no passage) Question f(x) = 8,000(0.81)^(x/6) The function f gives the value, in dollars, of a vehicle after x months of use. If the value of the vehicle decreases each year by p% of its value the preceding year, what is the value of p?
question: Passage (no passage) Question f(x) = 8,000(0.81)^(x/6) The function f gives the value, in dollars, of a vehicle after x months of use. If the value of the vehicle decreases each year by p% of its value the preceding year, what is the value of p?
rationale: Explanation written by Claude. Step 1: Identify what the base and the exponent mean. In f(x) = 8,000(0.81)^(x/6), the variable x is measured in months . The exponent x/6 increases by 1 every 6 months, so 0.81 is the factor by which the value is multiplied per 6 months , not per year. Step 2: Convert to a yearly factor. One year = 12 months, so the exponent grows by 12/6 = 2. The yearly multiplier is Step 3: Turn the retained fraction into a percent decrease. Keeping 0.6561 of the value means losing Rounded to the nearest whole number, p = 34. Answer C. Step 4: Rule out the traps. B (19) — computes 1 − 0.81 = 19%. This is the decrease per 6-month period, not per year. It ignores the /6 in the exponent entirely. This is the single most common trap on this item. D (81) — reads 0.81 as the percent lost rather than the fraction retained . The base of an exponential in this form is always the multiplier that survives, so 0.81 means 81% remains and 19% is lost. A (9) — roughly half of 19; it comes from taking the 19% figure and dividing by a period count instead of compounding. Percent change never scales linearly across periods; it compounds, which is why the annual figure (34%) is more than 19%, not less. Rule to carry forward: with b^(x/k), the base b applies once per k units of x. To get the rate per unit-of-time T, raise b to (T/k) first, then subtract from 1. rationale: Step 1: Analyze the relationship. The sentence is describing the size of the maze by providing a result: the fact that ten soccer fields can fit inside it. We need to connect the adjective large to the result clause ten full-sized soccer fields could fit inside it using the correct grammatical structure. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Name what the blank must do. English expresses "degree + consequence" with the fixed pair so … that or enough … that . The word that is a subordinating conjunction here: it turns the following independent clause into a subordinate result clause attached to enough . Without it, two independent clauses sit side by side with no connector. Step 3: Eliminate C. "is large enough ten full-sized soccer fields could fit inside it" — nothing links the two clauses. Run-on (fused sentence). Step 4: Eliminate A. "is large enough, ten full-sized soccer fields could fit inside it" — a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses. Comma splice. Step 5: Eliminate B. "enough, that" has the right connector but punctuates it wrongly. A subordinating that introducing a required complement is never separated from the word it completes by a comma — the result clause is restrictive, not parenthetical. Step 6: Confirm D. "is large enough that ten full-sized soccer fields could fit inside it" — enough that correctly subordinates the result clause with no stray punctuation, and the rest of the sentence continues with "and the site … relies on wind power." passage: Passage (no passage) Question 49x² + kx + 36 = 0 In the given equation, k is a constant. For which of the following values of k will the equation have more than one real solution?
question: Passage (no passage) Question 49x² + kx + 36 = 0 In the given equation, k is a constant. For which of the following values of k will the equation have more than one real solution?
rationale: Explanation written by Claude. Step 1: Translate "more than one real solution" into a condition. For ax² + bx + c = 0, the number of real solutions is governed by the discriminant D = b² − 4ac: D > 0 → two distinct real solutions D = 0 → exactly one real solution (a double root) D < 0 → no real solutions "More than one" means strictly two, so we need D > 0 . Step 2: Compute the threshold. Here a = 49, c = 36, b = k: So the equation has two real solutions exactly when k < −84 or k > 84. Step 3: Test each choice against |k| > 84. A: k = −90 → |−90| = 90 > 84. ✓ D = 8100 − 7056 = 1044 > 0. Two real solutions. Correct. B: k = −84 → |−84| = 84, which is not greater than 84. D = 7056 − 7056 = 0, a perfect square trinomial (7x + 6)² = 0 with the single root x = −6/7. Exactly one solution — this is the trap, since it satisfies the boundary but the question asked for more than one. C: k = 20 → 400 − 7056 = −6656 < 0. No real solutions. D: k = 80 → 6400 − 7056 = −656 < 0. No real solutions. Close to the threshold but still short — 84, not 80, is the cutoff. Rule to carry forward: "more than one real solution" = strict inequality D > 0. Any choice that makes D exactly 0 is a deliberate trap, and negative k values count just as well as positive ones because the discriminant squares b. question: Passage Poetry embraced portrayals of awe-inspiring, momentous, and intimidating experiences of nature at the height of the nineteenth century Romantic Era, only to rediscover such "sublime" experiences in a much different context—the Postmodern twentieth century. Exemplary here is Sylvia Plath's 1962 poem "Blackberrying." Here, the text's speaker begins by picking blackberries in a somewhat unassuming manner. Then, the poem shifts emphasis, as the speaker moves towards the sea and observes an impersonal "great space" opening in nature—exactly the sort of daunting impression that Romanticism associated with the sublime. Question Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Like Romantic Era poets, Postmodern poets such as Sylvia Plath emphasized the sublime.
Plath's "Blackberrying" enters into an intentional contrast with some Romantic Era poetry.
A dramatic shift in tone occurs as the poem Blackberrying progresses.
Plath's poetry as a whole depicts everyday events as disorienting.
answer: ["A \u2014 Like Romantic Era poets, Postmodern poets such as Sylvia Plath emphasized the sublime."]
rationale: Step 1: Identify the core claim. The passage begins by establishing a connection between two different literary eras: the nineteenth-century Romantic Era and the Postmodern twentieth century. It notes that Postmodern poetry "rediscovered" the Romantic concept of the sublime (awe-inspiring or daunting nature). Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Note the structural role of the example. "Exemplary here is Sylvia Plath's 1962 poem" signals that everything after it is evidence for the opening claim, not a new claim. The final clause closes the loop explicitly: the "great space" is "exactly the sort of daunting impression that Romanticism associated with the sublime." The passage's argument is continuity across eras, not contrast. Step 3: Eliminate B. Wrong polarity. B says Plath contrasts with Romantic poetry; the passage says she rediscovers the same sublime. The only contrast mentioned is of context ("a much different context"), not of aesthetic aim. Step 4: Eliminate C. True but too narrow. The tonal shift from berry-picking to "great space" is a supporting detail inside the example. A main-idea answer must cover the era-to-era claim in the first sentence, which C never touches. Step 5: Eliminate D. Out of scope and overreaching. The passage discusses one 1962 poem, not "Plath's poetry as a whole," and never characterizes everyday events as disorienting — the daunting impression comes from the sea and open space, not the ordinary act of picking blackberries. Step 6: Confirm A. A states both halves of the passage: Postmodern poets (Plath) emphasized the sublime, like the Romantics. That is the claim the example exists to prove. Rule to carry forward: on main-idea questions, the answer must match the sentence the example is serving — an option describing only what happens inside the example (like C) is a detail, and an option flipping the relationship (like B) is a polarity trap. question: Passage When river ecologists assess how pollutants alter freshwater mussel behavior, they often introduce controlled chemical stimuli to isolate specific stress responses. In a recent experiment, Dr. Maya Ellsworth of the University of Minnesota incorporated the food-grade _ into test tanks to evaluate whether trace additives that normally pass unnoticed in waterways might nonetheless affect mussels' ability to clamp their shells under sudden environmental shifts. rationale: Step 1: Analyze the noun phrase. The sentence discusses a specific chemical substance: sodium benzoate. In the phrase "the food-grade preservative sodium benzoate," the name sodium benzoate specifies which "food-grade preservative" is being used. This is called a restrictive appositive. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Apply the restrictive/non-restrictive rule. A restrictive appositive — one that narrows a general noun down to a particular referent — takes no commas. A non-restrictive appositive (extra, droppable information) is fenced off with a pair of commas. "Food-grade preservative" is generic; there are many. The name is doing identifying work, so it is restrictive and takes no punctuation. Step 3: Check the sentence frame. The blank sits inside "incorporated the food-grade _ into test tanks." The noun phrase is the direct object of incorporated and is immediately followed by the prepositional phrase into test tanks . Nothing may separate a verb from its object, or the object from the preposition that completes the thought. Step 4: Eliminate C and B. Both end the blank with a comma, cutting the direct object off from "into test tanks": "incorporated the food-grade preservative sodium benzoate, into test tanks." A comma never separates an object from the prepositional phrase that follows it. B compounds the error by also inserting an opening comma. Step 5: Eliminate D. "the food-grade preservative, sodium benzoate into test tanks" opens a non-restrictive appositive but never closes it. Paired commas must come in twos; a single leading comma leaves the sentence unbalanced. (Even if it were closed, the appositive is restrictive here, so commas would be wrong regardless.) Step 6: Confirm A. "incorporated the food-grade preservative sodium benzoate into test tanks" — clean noun phrase, no punctuation intruding between the object and its preposition. Rule to carry forward: name-after-category ("the poet Sylvia Plath," "the preservative sodium benzoate") is restrictive → zero commas. Also, if a choice adds one comma but not its partner, it is wrong on structure alone. Reading & Writing · Medium · Standard English Conventions · Boundaries

question: Passage The following text is adapted from Christina Rossetti's 1876 poem "Twilight Calm." One by one the flowers close, Lily and dewy rose Shutting their tender petals from the moon: The grasshoppers are still; but not so soon Are still the noisy crows. The dormouse squats and eats Choice little dainty bits Beneath the spreading roots of a broad lime; Nibbling his fill he stops from time to time And listens where he sits. Question As used in the text, what does the word "bits" most nearly mean?
rationale: Step 1: Analyze the context. The text describes a dormouse that squats and eats something described as "Choice little dainty bits." The next lines mention the dormouse "Nibbling his fill," which strongly suggests that bits refers to small pieces of food. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Define what the blank demands. Substitute into the line: "The dormouse squats and eats choice little dainty ___." The word must name a physical, edible thing, and the modifiers choice , little , and dainty all point to something small and appetizing. Anything that is not food fails immediately. Step 3: Eliminate A — Examples. "Bits" can mean instances in ordinary usage ("bits of evidence"), but a dormouse cannot eat an example. Right dictionary entry, wrong sense for this context. Step 4: Eliminate C — Moments. "Bits" does mean short spans of time ("wait a bit"), and the poem even uses "from time to time" two lines later, which makes this tempting. But eats takes a physical object, and "dainty moments" is not something to nibble. This is the trap for readers who match the nearby word time instead of the governing verb. Step 5: Eliminate D — Extracts. An extract is a portion drawn out of a larger source — a passage from a book or a concentrated substance (vanilla extract). Neither sense fits scraps a mouse forages under a lime tree; nothing is being drawn out of anything. Right general family (a part of a whole) but wrong register and wrong process. Step 6: Confirm B — Morsels. A morsel is precisely a small, tasty piece of food. It carries the same connotation as choice and dainty and pairs naturally with nibbling . Rule to carry forward: on words-in-context, let the verb pick the sense. Here eats forces a concrete edible noun, which kills three of four choices before you weigh nuance. question: Passage Protein-based treatments at the cellular level guide the development of measures to mitigate problems such as heart disease. _ John Elrod and Joanne Garbincius have studied the mitochondrial proteins NCLX and TMEM65 not simply for the sake of intellectual interest but because understanding these proteins could help to prevent heart failure. Question Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
rationale: Step 1: Analyze the relationship. The first sentence states a general principle: protein-based treatments are used to mitigate heart disease. The second sentence provides a specific example: researchers study two proteins specifically because they could help prevent heart failure. The second sentence directly applies the logic introduced in the first. Remaining steps written by Claude (OnePrep's were locked). Step 2: Name the required relationship. General principle → specific case that follows from it. That is consequence / application , not contrast, not broadening, not correction. The transition must signal "and so, following that principle…" Step 3: Eliminate A — More broadly speaking. Wrong direction of movement. "More broadly" signals zooming out to a wider claim, but sentence 2 zooms in to two named proteins and two named researchers. Movement from general to specific cannot be flagged as a widening. Step 4: Eliminate C — On the other hand. Wrong polarity. This signals contrast or an opposing consideration, but nothing in sentence 2 opposes sentence 1 — the researchers' motive ("could help to prevent heart failure") is exactly what sentence 1 predicts. Step 5: Eliminate D — Rather. Rather corrects or replaces a preceding statement ("not X; rather, Y"). Sentence 1 is not being retracted or corrected. Note the passage already contains its own "not simply … but" correction inside sentence 2; Rather at the front would wrongly aim that corrective force at sentence 1. Step 6: Confirm B — By this logic. It marks sentence 2 as an application of the reasoning just established: because protein work at the cellular level guides heart-disease treatment, these two researchers pursue these two proteins for therapeutic reasons. Rule to carry forward: classify the two sentences' relationship before looking at the choices, then reject on category (contrast / correction / broadening / application). Transitions questions are almost always decided by category, not by which one "sounds smoother." Reading & Writing · Medium · Expression of Ideas · Transitions
